title: CS102_Unit1d_Unit_Objectives
summary: Lists the learning objectives for the unit: comparison operators, if statement syntax, and tracing program execution.
main_text:
Unit Objectives:
- Know the comparison operators
- Know the syntax of an if..else if..else statement and which parts are required and which are optional

title: CS102_Unit1d_Outline
summary: Overview of the topics covered in this unit: comparison operators, the three forms of conditional statements, and compound conditionals.
main_text:
Outline:
- Comparison operators
- Conditional statements (3 forms): if statements, if..else statements, if..else if..else statements
- Compound conditional statements: AND, OR, and NOT (&&, ||, !) operators

title: CS102_Unit1d_Control_Structures
summary: Introduces the concept of control structures as language constructs that let a program make decisions, listing if, switch, while, and for.
main_text:
We need ways of making decisions in our program:
- To repeat code until we want it to stop
- To only execute certain code if a condition is true
- To execute one segment of code or another

Language constructs that allow us to make decisions are referred to as control structures. The common ones are:
- if statements
- switch statements (Not covered nor necessary in this class)
- while loops (Unit 2)
- for loops (Unit 2)
notes_text: switch statements are explicitly excluded from course scope; while and for loops are deferred to Unit 2.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Making_Decisions
summary: Explains the conceptual pipeline from comparisons to conditions to decisions, showing how simple/compound conditions built from comparisons drive code execution via if statements.
main_text:
Comparison of values results in 'true' or 'false' results (e.g. x > 0). Using comparisons we can develop simple or compound conditions:
- If usc_wins >= 12 we will play for the championship
- If x > 0 AND y > 0, take some action

Using conditions we can make decisions about what code to execute:
if(x > 0 AND y > 0)

This illustrates the conceptual pipeline: Comparisons (true/false) -> Conditions -> Decisions (if..else).

images.description: A vertical flowchart showing the conceptual pipeline of decision-making in code: Comparisons (true/false) feed into Conditions, which feed into Decisions (if..else), connected by downward arrows through three stacked boxes.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Comparison_Operators
summary: Presents the six basic C/C++ comparison operators with their meanings and code examples.
main_text:
To perform comparison of variables, constants, or expressions in C/C++ we can use the basic 6 comparison operators:
- == : Equality, e.g. if(x == y)
- != : Inequality, e.g. if(x != 7)
- < : Less-than, e.g. if(x < 0)
- > : Greater-than, e.g. if(y > x)
- <= : Less-than OR equal to, e.g. if(x <= -3)
- >= : Greater-than OR equal to, e.g. if(y >= 2)

images.description: A reference table listing all six C/C++ comparison operators alongside their meaning and a short code example for each.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Warmup_Self-Learning
summary: A self-directed learning activity prompting students to use an AI tool to ask a paraphrased question about if statements based on their prior programming experience level.
main_text:
Use an AI tool to ask (paraphrase) one of the questions below based on your experience and then read/learn from its response:
- Just starting to learn programming: 'List the most pertinent facts I need to know when learning about if statements in C++?'
- Reasonable experience in a language other than C++ (e.g., Python): 'What are the major differences about the syntax and meaning of if statements in C++ compared to a language like Python?'
- Reasonable experience in another language: 'What are some of the most common mistakes when using if statements in C++?'
notes_text: This is a self-learning exercise encouraging use of AI tools tailored to the student's existing programming background.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Conditional_Execution_-_if
summary: Introduces the basic if statement: its purpose, syntax, control-flow diagram, and a worked example that converts a negative number to positive.
notes_text: The example demonstrates converting a negative input to its absolute value using a single if block.

images.description: A flowchart depicting the flow of control for a basic if statement: a decision diamond/branch for condition1 leads to 'If Block Statements' when true, or skips directly to 'Following statements' when false, with numbered annotations (1, 2, 3) mapping to lines of the adjacent code sample.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Conditional_Execution_-_if_else
summary: Introduces the if..else statement, explaining that else is always optional and creates a mutually exclusive code execution structure, with a control-flow diagram, annotated code, and a fork-in-the-road illustration.

images.description: A flowchart with a decision diamond for 'condition' branching True to an 'If Block Statements' box and False to an 'Else Block Statements' box, both merging downward into a 'Following statements' box, with numbered call-outs (1,2,3) linking to the code panel.

A photo illustration of a road forking into two diverging paths under a sunset sky, with overlay labels marking one path 'if' and the other 'else', visually symbolizing the two mutually exclusive branches of an if..else statement.

title: CS102_Unit1d_If_Else_If_Else
summary: Explains the if..else if..else chain for handling more than two cases, noting that else if is optional and can repeat any number of times, illustrated with a train-car analogy and full code structure.
notes_text: The train analogy: the 'if' is the locomotive (required), 'else if' cars are optional and repeatable, and the 'else' caboose is optional and must come last.

images.description: An illustration of a toy train where the locomotive represents the required 'if', two identical middle cars represent repeatable optional 'else if' blocks, and the red caboose represents the optional trailing 'else' block, with a bracket labeled 'optional' spanning the else-if and else cars.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Pick_the_Right_Structure
summary: Compares the output of a chain of independent if statements versus an if..else if..else chain for the same grade value of 95, showing that independent ifs can all execute while else-if chains execute only one branch.
notes_text: Key takeaway: independent if statements can all fire (multiple ranges printed for grade=95), while an if..else if..else chain guarantees only one branch executes.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Common_Style_Mistake
summary: Warns against using multiple independent if statements when an if..else structure is more appropriate, since it is less readable and more error-prone even though not functionally wrong.

title: CS102_Unit1d_What_Goes_In_an_if_/_else_Block
summary: Demonstrates that any valid C++ code (expressions, assignments, function calls, even nested if..else) can be placed inside if/else blocks, using a full example program computing a square root.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Logical_Operators
summary: Introduces the three logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) used to build compound conditions in C++, with symbols and example syntax.
main_text:
We can create compound conditions by using the logical AND, OR, and NOT operators:
- && : AND, e.g. if( (x==0) && (y==0) )
- || : OR, e.g. if( (x < 0) || (y < 0) )
- ! : NOT, e.g. if( !x )

images.description: A reference table listing the three logical operators (&&, ||, !) with their meaning and a code example for each.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Logical_AND_OR_NOT
summary: Shows the truth tables for the AND, OR, and NOT logical operations, illustrating how each evaluates across all combinations of true/false inputs.
main_text:
The following tables show how the logical operations are evaluated under any set of values.

AND: All inputs must be true for the resulting expression to be true; if even one is false, the condition is false.
OR: If any input is true, the condition evaluates to true.

AND truth table (A, B -> result): False/False->False, False/True->False, True/False->False, True/True->True.
OR truth table (A, B -> result): False/False->False, False/True->True, True/False->True, True/True->True.
NOT truth table (A -> result): False->True, True->False.

images.description: Three small truth tables side by side showing the output of AND, OR, and NOT operations for all combinations of boolean inputs A and B.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Order_of_Evaluation_Precedence
summary: Explains operator precedence among logical operators (! highest, then &&, then || lowest) and recommends explicit parenthesization, illustrated with an ambiguous vs. explicitly parenthesized code example.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Common_Mistakes_1
summary: Warns about two common beginner mistakes: confusing the assignment operator (=) with the equality operator (==), and using multiple independent if statements instead of if..else.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Common_Mistakes_2
summary: Warns that all conditions must be formulated as pairwise comparisons, showing invalid chained-comparison and combined-value syntax versus their corrected forms.
notes_text: This addresses a subtle C++ pitfall: chained comparisons like '0 <= x <= 9' compile but do not do what students expect, since they evaluate left-to-right as separate boolean operations.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Rule_Exception_Idiom
summary: Introduces the Rule/Exception idiom: performing a default action before an if statement, then using the if to correct exceptional cases, illustrated with a shipping fee and a manager bonus example.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Rule_Exception_Idiom_2
summary: Shows that the rule/exception idiom (default value plus corrective if) is often equivalent to using an if..else structure, comparing both versions of the shipping fee example.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Decision_Tree_Subcase_Idiom
summary: Introduces the Subcase (decision tree) idiom using nested if statements to further divide a case into subcases, illustrated with a customer service call menu tree.
notes_text: The customer service call menu diagram models this idiom: top-level cases (Account Issues, Hours of Operation) branch further into sub-cases (Balance, Cancel) under Account Issues.

images.description: A hierarchical tree diagram representing a customer service phone menu, with top-level branches for 'Account Issues' and 'Hours of Operation', and sub-branches 'Balance' and 'Cancel' nested under 'Account Issues', illustrating how nested if statements model layered decision cases.

title: CS102_Unit1d_Digging_Deeper_Structural_OR_and_AND
summary: Explains how nested if statements form a structural AND relationship, and how if..else if chains performing the same action can be replaced by an OR condition, with four side-by-side code comparisons.
notes_text: This slide connects the logical operators (&&, ||) directly to their structural code equivalents (nested ifs for AND, combined else-if branches for OR).

title: CS102_Unit1d_Comparing_Floating_Point_Doubles_Numbers
summary: Explains why exact equality comparison of doubles is unreliable due to rounding errors, and demonstrates the correct approach of comparing the absolute difference against a small epsilon.
notes_text: This is a foundational numerical-computing caveat: floating point rounding error means direct equality checks on doubles are unreliable; epsilon-based comparison is the standard fix.
